items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' The greeting went straight to business — 'Einstein Moving Company, this is Eric' then 'Yeah, sure thing. Did you have a specific date in mind?' The warmth arrived later and never stopped, but the opening thirty seconds had none of it.

The agenda statement came two-thirds of the way into the call and had no 'sound good?' attached. 'what I'd like to do is just kind of break down the pricing structure for you, talk to you about kind of what goes into our hourly rate then about how our clock works and lastly talk to you about your estimate' is a genuine roadmap — the best-structured one in this week's sample — but it arrived at minute twelve, it covered only the back half of the call, it carried no timeframe, and it ended with a period instead of a question. The customer supplied her own confirmation ('Okay, great') because she was never asked for one. That is the difference between a 5/7 and a 7/7 on this section, and it is why the agenda flag reads false on a call that nearly earned it.

Packing service was never offered. He asked about box count but never asked whether she wanted help packing, on a customer who volunteered 'I'm a little bit like overwhelmed with like the amount of stuff that I have.' That is an explicit buying signal for a packing upsell and it went unanswered.
'Pricing is super simple' opener never used.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. 'this will cover the taxes for your move as well as the insurance for your move' was the entire coverage conversation — the word insurance inside a list. No brand name, no $2,000, no repair-replace-reimburse, no 60c/lb baseline. This customer specifically flagged an heirloom: 'a chest that is from my grandfather so it's really big' and a 'Mid-Century modern like old cat like dresser' that is 'very, very heavy.' Erik captured both in the inventory and coded the chest as antique, then never told her what happens if one of them gets damaged. That is the most valuable unsaid sentence on the call.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned — on a call where the customer spent two minutes explaining that her cat is unfriendly, will be screaming from the bathroom, and that strangers in the apartment are the thing she is nervous about. The pre-move email with the crew's names and photos is the direct answer to 'who is coming into my home,' and Erik instead answered with a general reassurance about the team being outgoing.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, despite Erik pinning a specific arrival window — '8:30 AM to 9:00 AM' — for a customer who took the entire day off work.

The no-hidden-fees claim was strong but not the full pitch. 'there are absolutely no additional fees or hidden fees of any type even if we choose to take the stairs on move day, you're not charged for that. So absolutely nothing outside of that $206' is well-targeted at a real concern, but it never itemizes — no credit card fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees.

The clock explanation never said when the clock starts. The 2.5-hour minimum and the fifteen-minute proration both landed cleanly, but the customer was never told that billable time begins on-site when the contract opens. On a move going down the street, whether the drive between the two complexes is on her clock is a live question and it was never answered.

No sense-check anywhere on the call. Not once — not after the pricing block, not after the clock, not after the estimate. Eighteen minutes, three substantial explanations, and no 'does that make sense?' The customer filled the gaps herself with 'Okay, great' and 'Okay, perfect,' which is generous of her and not the same thing.

No equivalents or plain-language anchors. Erik measured the walks in feet at four separate points — 75 feet at the origin, 20 to 25 at the destination — which is excellent data capture, but he never translated any of it for the customer. A school-bus reference or similar would have made those numbers mean something to someone who told him outright 'I don't know measurements.'
Truck count never explicitly stated. 'the truck that they're driving' appears inside the what's-included list; the customer never heard 'one truck.'

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10, and this is the single largest point loss on an otherwise strong call. The customer handed him the setup twice, unprompted. First: 'there's some stuff that I think I'll probably be able to move cause I'm getting in there a little bit earlier to like slowly move some stuff over there.' Then again: 'for the most part I'm kind of planning on moving stuff slowly over there, piece by piece. So, since it's down the street, I don't have to like.' Erik's responses were 'Oh, you're so lucky' and 'Yeah, no, no, like, jumping through hoops for it. Yeah, that's nice.' He validated the behavior and never converted it — never said it comes off her clock, never gave her the consolidation list, never said 'take a carload,' never closed with a sense-check. She was already doing the highest-value thing a customer can do and nobody told her it was worth money.
No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email. 'it should have everything broken down for you in there' is close and it is not the same instruction.

No 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. 'If there's any questions concerns or comments you have about the estimate or the confirmation there. Just give me a holler' invites feedback but routes it away from the email and frames it as questions rather than corrections. This is the closest near-miss on the email-handoff flag in the sample and it still does not meet the bar.
No explicit 'any other questions before I let you go?' — the standing invitation to 'give me a holler' was offered in the sign-off instead of a direct solicitation.
No hours and no direct number or email address given at close.
Ecobox or Sparefoot referral never offered, on a customer who described herself as overwhelmed and who has ten boxes of vinyl records she called 'very heavy.'

Eighteen and a half minutes is long for a 700-square-foot one-bedroom moving 'literally down the street.' Some of that is the thoroughness that makes this call good, but a meaningful stretch is dead air hunting an address — 'Why does it given me I don't want US... Is it, is it Florence Avenue or Florence road... Lawrence Avenue... There we go. Let's see if that's the one. There we go. Okay, I was like, yeah, I can't find it. Okay, gotcha, alrighty, it was giving me like Fort Worth you live Arlington. I was like, no, no, no' — narrated out loud to the customer.
top_strength: This is the best discovery call in the sample and the reason is that Erik treats the estimate as something he builds rather than something he asserts. He measured the walk at four separate points and did it without making it feel like an interrogation: 'thinking about where we would be parking on ground floor. How far of a walk? Would you say it is to say the elevator,' then 'once we get to the second floor, how far from the elevator is your front door?' — and when the customer said she did not know measurements, he did not drop it, he closed the loop himself: 'I'll put you down for maybe about 75 feet in total, that's, you know, with the, with the ground and then on the second floor there.' He repeated the entire sequence at the destination, including the correct operational judgment out loud — 'we typically take the closer option unless it's pretty similar' — when she told him the stairs were next to her unit but the elevator was far. He then walked the inventory item by item ('would you kind of walk me through just item by, item what we have there?'), caught the two pieces that actually change the hours, and coded one of them correctly on the spot: 'Oh, okay, would you say it's kind of antique. Maybe just with the, with the grandfather.' He asked the moving-stressor question verbatim and at the right moment — 'Are there any specific stresser or concerns you have about the moving process or maybe just this move-in particular?' — and when the answer was a long, slightly embarrassed story about an unfriendly cat on medication, he did the thing that separates a 5 from a 3 on presence: he thanked her for it, made it operational, and made it lighter. 'I've got some notes in there which truthfully, I think that's a great thing that you shared... I'll get a note in there just be mindful of that... we'll try to make this as seamless as possible for you,' and then 'Maybe he'll be a nice cat when you guys move.' She laughed it off and gave him the rest of the logistics unprompted. The estimate itself is the cleanest in this week's batch: 2.5 to 3.5 hours with the typical-range justification ('It's pretty standard for us to see a one bedroom taking that amount of time'), both dollar ends stated so she could see the spread ('if the two man team there would have, were to take the full three and a half hours to move you would see a cost of $721, if they were to be closer to the minimum there that 2.5 hour mark, we'd be looking at about $515'), and no padding anywhere — he did not pull it up to be safe. The booking attempt and the no-deposit delivery are also the strongest in the sample and they arrived together, in the right order: 'we do have availability like, we had talked about on the eighteenth for you that Friday. If you wanted to secure something there's no deposit required to book with us and then if something does come up and you need to reschedule or cancel, it's also free of cost to do that. Did you want to go ahead and grab a spot today?' She said yes immediately. He then re-verified her email letter by letter before hanging up: 'I know you gave me the email at the beginning of the call but I just wanna verify I have the right email.'
coaching_note: Erik is close to a mastery-track call and three specific things are holding it at 54. First and largest: Save Your Ass is a zero on the most Save-Your-Ass-ready customer of the week. She told him twice she is already carrying things over herself, and both times he praised it instead of pricing it. The line was right there: 'Melissa, that's actually the best thing you can do — every load you take over yourself comes straight off our clock. Keep going with the small stuff, the loose things in drawers, whatever's on the walls, the closet odds and ends. If the guys walk in and it's just the furniture and those ten boxes, you're landing at the bottom of that range instead of the top. Does that make sense?' That is worth ten points on the sheet, it is worth real money to her, and it is the behavior that most directly moves estimate accuracy — because a customer who pre-consolidates makes the 2.5-hour end of his own range the likely outcome instead of the optimistic one. Second: the differentiators. He landed the hourly rate, the inclusions, the free service zone and the no-deposit policy, and then said nothing about No Worries, Meet Your Mover, or the On-Time Guarantee. Two of those three were sitting on top of things the customer had already told him. She named an heirloom chest from her grandfather and a very heavy mid-century dresser — that is No Worries. She spent two minutes on her anxiety about strangers and an unfriendly cat — that is Meet Your Mover, and it is a better answer than 'the guys are pretty outgoing' because it puts names and faces on the strangers before move day. She took the whole day off for an 8:30 to 9:00 window — that is the On-Time Guarantee. Thirty seconds of differentiator content, aimed at things she had already volunteered, is the cheapest twelve points on this sheet. Third: sense-checks and the clock start. Zero 'does that make sense?' across eighteen minutes and three explanations, and the clock section never said when billable time begins. Add both — they are two sentences. On the agenda: the mid-call roadmap is genuinely the best-constructed in the sample and it still reads false on the flag, because a roadmap without a confirmation ask is a monologue preview. Move it to the top of the call, add the timeframe, and put a question mark on the end: 'I'll get some details about your move, then walk you through pricing and your estimate — about ten to fifteen minutes. Sound good?' That single edit converts the closest near-miss of the week into a hit. No estimate-accuracy flag on this call, and that is worth saying explicitly to the bottom-4 group: Erik quoted 2.5 to 3.5 hours for a 700-square-foot one-bedroom, stated it was the typical range for the home size, gave both dollar ends, and did not pad it upward to be safe. That is what the target behavior looks like and this call is the one to play in the calibration session.
phone_presence_notes: Name used naturally four times across the call rather than bolted onto the greeting ('Perfect, Melissa,' 'everything is checking out Melissa,' 'absolutely everything that you need Melissa from head to tow'), real reciprocal humor in both directions — his daughter yelling in the background, her cat knocking a toy around, 'Maybe he'll be a nice cat when you guys move' — and he converted her most vulnerable moment into a job note and a compliment ('truthfully, I think that's a great thing that you shared'); the customer ended with 'Thank you so much, I appreciate it' and had already booked.
